rules.text: If the query image contains prominent specular highlights (glare), bubbles, or mucus that could be mistaken for lesions, trust A (Agent) as it is better at distinguishing these artifacts from true pathology.

If the query image shows a small, isolated, pale, rounded feature near a sphincter or fold that resembles a polyp but is likely a normal anatomical variant, trust A (Agent) to correctly identify it as normal.

If the query image displays diffuse, circumferential erythema (redness), edema, or a granular texture affecting the entire mucosal surface, trust B (Direct) as it is more sensitive to widespread inflammatory conditions like colitis or esophagitis.
If the query image shows a dark, irregular, or depressed area that A (Agent) dismisses as a shadow or artifact, trust B (Direct) to correctly identify it as a pathological lesion (ulcer or tumor).
Mucosal surface is dominated by continuous pink, salmon, or light orange hues.
Surface texture is smooth or exhibits regular, continuous folds (rugae) without disruption.
No distinct, protruding, or sessile masses (polyps) are present on the mucosal surface.
No open, crater-like defects (ulcers) with raised or necrotic borders are visible.
Do not flag diffuse mucosal erythema or reddish hue as an ulcer if the surface texture remains smooth and intact.
Do not flag the Z-line (squamocolumnar junction) or gastric folds as a polypoid mass if they follow natural anatomical convergence.
Do not flag dark shadows, specular reflections, or bile staining as pigmented lesions or plaques.
